newsitem.title: UK: To infinity and beyond? Bonds look to technicals.
newsitem.headline: To infinity and beyond? Bonds look to technicals.

text.p: As European bond futures soar into uncharted territory and leave investors on unfamiliar soil, technical analysis can provide a map.
German, French and Italian debt futures have all broken through to all-time highs in recent trading.
"It's harder to define levels, but on the other hand, people are more keen to find and take notice of them," said David Sneddon, technical analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston.

On Tuesday, March German Bund futures on LIFFE shot past the previous record high of 102.99 set in December 1996, prompting some analysts to eye long-term continuation charts for clues to the next move.

Regina Neder, a broker at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Futures and Options in Frankfurt, cited a target of 103.38, a long-term trendline line linking the 1988 and 1994 highs, at 98.30 and 101.48, respectively.

That level was also popular for Fibonacci enthusiasts. In a Fibonacci number sequence, each number is the sum of the two preceeding numbers. Analysts use the ratios given by these numbers to provide the basis for analysis.

Bunds fell to a low of 99.28 on January 2, rallied to 101.92 on January 22 and then,retraced to 100.74 on January 28. The length of the first upmove, extended onto the pullback at 100.74, gives a target of 103.38.
Above there on Bund continuation charts,the market fell to 96.10 in early September, climbed to 102.99 in early December and then retraced back to 99.28.
A one-for-one projection sets a target of 106.17, while a 61.8-prcent Fibonacci projection puts resistance at 103.54.
March Bund futures were down 0.08 at 102.83 by 1425 GMT.
Robin Wilkin, senior technical analyst at MCM YieldWatch in London, said 99.28 was an obvious downside target.
"In the next four months, I would expect to see Bunds topping out and falling quickly to the 102.30 area, then moving sideways before really accelerating down," he said.

Analysts said investors were also looking more closely at stochastics, momentum indicators based on the idea that in a rising market, closing prices tend to cluster at the top of the price range. In a falling market, the opposite is true.
But for now, notionnel futures are oblivious to overbought signals on hourly and daily stochastics.
Steve Berry, technical analyst at NatWest Financial Futures in London said "the short-term stochastics are negative, but they aren't the best indicators in a strongly trending market."

March notionnel fell to 127.48 on January 3, rallied to 131.16 on January 22, and then corrected to 129.76 on January 28. That comes in just above 132.00. March futures were down four basis points at 131.60.
Above 132.00, the next obvious level was 132.24/26 and then 132.50, as analysts said the market tends to gravitate towards quarter, half, and round numbers when in new territory.

BTPs have lost some of their rampant upward pressure, backing off from the record high of 132.38 set in late January. A failure to hold above 132.00 will risk aborting the longer-term target, from the uptrend, at 135.00, analysts said.
Relying on round numbers, analysts said 132.50 was a target if the uptrend resumes. March BTPs were up 0.11 at 130.93.
